passage: Siddharth, you asked why I never studied what I loved. Sit, the diyas on your balcony can wait a minute. When I was fifteen, in Aligarh, every girl in my class signed up for the science stream, because Rukhsana did, and then her whole group did. I loved drawing buildings. I wanted arts, with geography. But standing alone at that form table, with thirty girls watching, my hands went cold. What if they laughed? What if I was the odd one out? So I ticked science. Two years of biology I hated. Rukhsana, it turned out, had only picked science because her cousin had. Much later, at twenty-four, I studied town planning anyway. So when your friends all pick the same thing, you remember Zeenat aunty's two lost years, hmm?

qa.q: Which stream did Zeenat really want at fifteen?
qa.a: Arts, with geography, because she loved drawing buildings.

qa.q: What was young Zeenat feeling at the form table?
qa.a: She felt anxious and exposed, afraid the thirty girls would laugh if she stood out, so ticking science felt safer.

qa.q: What choice at the form table could have changed the story?
qa.a: She could have ticked arts with geography, perhaps after talking to a teacher or family member beforehand, so the choice rested on what she loved rather than on the crowd.

qa.q: Why did Rukhsana pick science, according to the story?
qa.a: Rukhsana had only picked science because her cousin had, so even the person everyone followed was following someone else.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing a study stream because many peers did, and feeling anxious about standing out.

passage: By the second week of December, the student union election had taken over the Leeds campus. Everywhere Nkechi looked, people wore the same orange badge for Callum, the candidate with the catchy slogan. "Three thousand likes on his video," Liam said, pinning one to his scarf. "They can't all be wrong." Nkechi hadn't read a single manifesto. On the way to the library she passed Callum's stall, giant orange balloons bobbing in the wind and a queue for free hot chocolate. At the voting booth she hesitated, pen above the paper. She knew nothing about the other two names. Orange badges filled the corridor behind her. She ticked Callum. It felt like joining a warm crowd on a cold day. Later, in the library, she finally opened his manifesto. It was mostly the slogan, repeated.

qa.q: What did Callum's stall offer?
qa.a: Free hot chocolate, with giant orange balloons bobbing in the wind.

qa.q: Why did voting for Callum feel right to Nkechi at the booth?
qa.a: With orange badges everywhere, she felt reassured and part of a warm crowd, assuming that so many people could not be wrong.

qa.q: What could Nkechi do before the next vote?
qa.a: Read each candidate's manifesto and decide what she thinks of the ideas, treating popularity as a reason to check rather than as proof.

qa.q: How does Liam see the badges and likes?
qa.a: Liam treats the three thousand likes as proof and pins on a badge without seeming to ask why Callum is popular.

grounding: Shows a young adult voting for a candidate because he is popular, assuming that many people cannot be wrong.

passage: When the coaching centre in Rampur opened a batch for the police constable exam, it felt as if every young person in Himani's village signed up. Lavanya came by with two forms. "Everyone's going, Himani. Fill it, we'll take the same bus." Himani sat with the form on the verandah while the buffaloes shifted in the yard. She asked herself two questions. Why do I want this? Mostly, she admitted, because everyone else is going. And if nobody in the village would ever know what I chose, what would I pick? The answer came quickly: the nursing assistant course at the district hospital, which she had wanted since Dadi's long illness. The next morning she handed the constable form back to Lavanya. "Save me a seat on the bus anyway," she said, smiling. "We'll ride together as far as the hospital stop."

qa.q: Which course did Himani choose?
qa.a: The nursing assistant course at the district hospital.

qa.q: What did Himani feel after honestly asking why she wanted the constable exam?
qa.a: Admitting it was mostly because everyone else was going left her calm and clear-headed rather than pulled along.

qa.q: Which question helped Himani most, and why?
qa.a: Asking what she would pick if nobody would ever know, because it removed the pull of the crowd and showed her real wish.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel when Himani hands back the form?
qa.a: Lavanya may feel a little disappointed at first, but reassured by Himani's warmth and the plan to ride the bus together 🙂

grounding: Shows a person asking why she wants something and what she would choose if nobody knew, then leaving the crowd deliberately while staying connected.

subtype: Teacher or elder is always right [Actor]
passage: In the monsoon, spiders crept into the village school near Madikeri to escape the rain, and one had spun a web across the window. "Look, children, another insect," Aparna ma'am said, pointing with her ruler. Payal stared at it. She had just counted its legs: eight. Her science book, open on her lap, said in a box that insects have six legs and spiders are not insects. Her heart thumped. Aparna ma'am was the cleverest person in the village; she even helped Payal's father read letters from the bank. Maybe the book was wrong. Maybe Payal had counted badly. She shut the book quietly. When ma'am asked, "Everyone understood?" Payal nodded with the others, her cheeks warm, and copied "spider = insect" into her notebook.

qa.q: How many legs did Payal count on the spider?
qa.a: Eight.

qa.q: Why did Payal shut the book instead of asking?
qa.a: She admired Aparna ma'am so much, and felt so afraid of questioning her, that doubting her own counting felt safer than doubting the teacher.

qa.q: What small step could Payal take?
qa.a: She could show the box in the book to Aparna ma'am after class and ask, "Ma'am, can you help me understand this?"

qa.q: How might Aparna ma'am respond if Payal showed her the book?
qa.a: A caring teacher might feel a moment's surprise, then be pleased that Payal read so carefully, and correct the notes for the whole class.

grounding: Shows a child accepting a teacher's statement even when her book and her own counting contradict it, too afraid to question.

passage: Last Christmas break, our school debate team trained every morning in the empty staff room, and Manoj sir ran everything. He had been a state champion once; we all practically worshipped him. On the third day he told me to open my speech with a "fact": that our country has the world's longest coastline. He said it so confidently that I wrote it down. That night I checked an atlas, and it said otherwise. I felt sick. Who was I to correct a state champion? The next morning I nearly stayed quiet. Then I said, very badly, "Sir, sorry, um, I think the atlas says... not us?" My face went hot. He frowned, checked, and laughed. "You're right, Himani. Good catch." I hadn't expected that. I've been checking things ever since, even when the person sounds very sure.

qa.q: What "fact" did Manoj sir tell Himani to open the speech with?
qa.a: That their country has the world's longest coastline.

qa.q: Why did Himani nearly stay quiet the next morning?
qa.a: Himani admired Manoj sir as a state champion and felt anxious and embarrassed about correcting him, as if a title made him automatically right.

qa.q: What helped Himani speak up, and what could make it easier next time?
qa.a: Having the atlas as evidence helped; next time Himani could show the source calmly and ask a question, keeping respect and truth together.

qa.q: How did Manoj sir react to being corrected?
qa.a: He frowned, checked, then laughed and said "Good catch," showing he cared more about accuracy than about always being right.

grounding: Shows a teenager weighing whether to trust a confident coach, and awkwardly learning that a title does not guarantee a fact is true.

passage:
Dear Anjali didi,
Eid Mubarak! Ammi sent sevaiyan to the site office and everyone loved it.
I need to tell you something I did. On Tuesday, Farooq sir, our senior engineer, handed me the scaffold checklist and said, "Just sign it, beta, I checked it this morning." I hadn't seen him go up. The top boards looked loose to me. But he has twenty years' experience, and everyone calls him Ustad. Saying "I'll check first" felt like calling him a liar. So I signed.
All afternoon my stomach hurt. At six I went back up and saw that two boards really were loose. I told the site safety officer, who closed that section and rang Farooq sir. He was annoyed, but the boards were fixed by morning.
Why was signing so easy and speaking up so hard?
Asif

qa.q: What did Farooq sir ask Asif to sign?
qa.a: The scaffold checklist.

qa.q: Why did Asif sign even though the boards looked loose?
qa.a: He admired and trusted Farooq sir's twenty years of experience, and questioning him felt disrespectful, like calling him a liar, so signing felt easier than speaking.

qa.q: What could Asif say next time to object politely?
qa.a: He could say, "Sir, I'd like to see it myself before I sign, so I learn," which keeps respect while refusing to sign something unchecked.

qa.q: How did Farooq sir react when the safety officer rang him?
qa.a: He was annoyed, but the loose boards were fixed by morning.

grounding: Shows a young trainee signing a senior's unchecked safety form because refusing felt disrespectful, before going back and reporting the danger.

passage:
Monday: At the planning meeting, Aadhya ma'am, the regional head everyone admired, announced that customers in small towns "don't want online ordering; they want to touch the product." Heads nodded around the table. Kunal had spent three months on that region's data. He said nothing yet, but wrote down her exact words.
Wednesday: Kunal asked for ten minutes with her. "Ma'am, I've learned a lot from you, and I'd like to understand how you reached that point about small towns." She described store visits from five years ago. Kunal then showed her his chart: online orders from those towns had tripled in two years. "I may be missing something," he added.
The following Monday: Aadhya ma'am opened the meeting with Kunal's chart on the screen. "I was working from old visits," she said. "We'll try online ordering in four towns first."

qa.q: What did Kunal's chart show?
qa.a: Online orders from those small towns had tripled in two years.

qa.q: What does Kunal's opening line on Wednesday suggest about his feelings towards Aadhya ma'am?
qa.a: He genuinely admires and respects her, and feels confident enough to question the idea without attacking her.

qa.q: Which steps made Kunal's challenge work?
qa.a: Asking how she reached the claim, showing his data politely, and admitting he might be missing something, so respect and disagreement stayed separate.

qa.q: How might Aadhya ma'am have felt looking at the chart?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and briefly uncomfortable, but secure enough to admit she had been working from old visits.

grounding: Shows a professional asking how a senior's claim was reached, offering evidence politely, and separating respect for her from agreeing with the idea.

passage: I've been on Zubin's team at the water board for two years, and I can tell you exactly when he changed. It was after the pipeline meeting in March. He'd asked, "Any concerns?" as always, and as always, eight of us stared at our notepads. Afterwards I saw him standing at the window for a long time, holding the minutes. At the next meeting he did something odd. Before saying what he thought, he went round the table: "Jyoti, what's the weakest part of this plan?" I nearly dropped my pen. I told him the Ward 6 valves were too old for the new pressure. He wrote it on the board and said, "Thank you. That's the most useful thing I've heard all week." Now people bring him bad news before lunch. I don't know what he was thinking at that window, but something clicked.

qa.q: What did Jyoti say was the weakest part of the plan?
qa.a: The Ward 6 valves were too old for the new pressure.

qa.q: What might Zubin have been feeling at the window after the March meeting?
qa.a: He may have felt troubled or uneasy, perhaps realising the team's silence came from his title rather than agreement, though Jyoti cannot be sure.

qa.q: What did Zubin change, and why did it work?
qa.a: He asked for the weakest part of the plan before giving his own view, and thanked people for bad news, so disagreeing felt safe and useful.

qa.q: What was it like for Jyoti to be asked directly?
qa.a: Jyoti was startled enough to nearly drop the pen, but then felt heard when the concern went on the board with a thank-you.

grounding: Shows a leader who notices staff never disagree, then invites criticism before sharing his own view and thanks people who bring bad news.

subtype: My friends are the good ones [Actor]
passage: On Winter Sports Day at the playschool, Miss gave everyone a cap: red or blue. Tejas got red. So did Kunal. By snack time, Tejas was sharing his orange slices only with red caps. "Blue caps are bad," he told Kunal. "They cheat." "Who cheated?" asked Miss. Tejas thought hard. "They just do." A girl in a blue cap held out her hand for a slice. Tejas hid the box behind his back. Yesterday, before the caps, she had been his swing partner.

qa.q: What colour cap did Tejas get?
qa.a: Tejas got a red cap.

qa.q: Why does Tejas say blue caps are bad?
qa.a: The red cap makes him feel proud and included in the red team, so the blue caps suddenly feel like outsiders, even his swing partner.

qa.q: How could Miss help the children after snack time?
qa.a: She could mix the teams for the next game and gently remind Tejas that his swing partner is the same friend in a different cap.

qa.q: How might the girl in the blue cap feel when Tejas hides the box?
qa.a: She probably feels confused and left out, since only yesterday she was his swing partner.

grounding: Shows a young child sharing only with his own cap colour and calling the other team bad, though the teams were random.

passage:
The evening after the winter house kabaddi final, Tushar burst into the kitchen.
"Green House won! We smashed Yellow!"
Shankar bhaiya, still in his yellow house T-shirt, looked up from his plate. "Your raider stepped out of the line twice."
"That was the mud. It was slippery."
"And when our raider stepped out?"
"That's cheating! Everyone saw!"
"Same mud, Tushar."
"It's different." Tushar grabbed a roti. "Yellow always cheats."
Dadaji chuckled from his chair. "In my school I was Blue House. We were sure Red always cheated. Sixty years later, my best friend is from Red House."
Tushar chewed slowly. "But Green is still the best."
"Of course it is," said Shankar bhaiya, rolling his eyes.

qa.q: Which house won the kabaddi final?
qa.a: Green House won, beating Yellow.

qa.q: Why does Tushar call Yellow's step-out cheating but Green's just mud?
qa.a: Winning with his own house makes him feel so proud that he excuses Green's fouls, while the same act from Yellow looks unfair to him.

qa.q: What could help Tushar judge the next match more fairly?
qa.a: He could ask what he would call a move if the other house did it, just like Shankar bhaiya's "Same mud" question.

qa.q: How does Shankar bhaiya see Tushar's cheering?
qa.a: Shankar bhaiya, from Yellow House, finds it unfair and a bit annoying that the same step-out counts as mud for Green and cheating for Yellow.

grounding: Shows a schoolchild cheering his own house, excusing its fouls and calling the same act cheating when another house does it.
